title: The Fewest Neighbour Swaps to Match Another Order

concept.title: Match equal colours in order, and the answer is the number of inversions of the matching
body: Beads in a row can be exchanged only with a **neighbour**. What is the fewest number of exchanges that turns the row `1 2 1 2` into `2 2 1 1`? Each exchange of two neighbours fixes at most one pair of beads that are in the wrong relative order, so the answer is the number of pairs that must be reversed, an **inversion count**.

With all colours different, give each bead of the present row the position it must reach in the wanted row. This gives a permutation `pos`, and the answer is the number of pairs `i < j` with `pos[i] > pos[j]`. When colours repeat, equal beads should never be swapped with each other (that wastes a move), so the **k-th bead of a colour in the present row is matched with the k-th bead of that colour in the wanted row**. After this matching the targets are all different again.

A Fenwick tree over the targets counts, for every bead, how many earlier beads have a larger target: that is `i` minus the earlier ones with a target at most `p`. The sum over all beads is the answer, up to about `n^2 / 2` (so use 64-bit numbers). Time O(n log n).

statement: A row of `n` beads has colours `a[1..n]`. In one move you may swap two beads that stand next to each other. Find the fewest moves that turn the row into the colours `b[1..n]` (the same colours, each the same number of times). Print this number.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of beads.
The second line has `n` colour numbers: the present order.
The third line has `n` colour numbers: the wanted order. It has the same colours as the present order, each the same number of times.
outputFormat: Print one number: the fewest moves.
constraints: The two orders contain the same colours with the same counts.

examples.note: Move the first 2 to the front (1 move: 2 1 1 2), then the last 2 to the second place (2 moves): 3 moves in total.

hints: A move that swaps two neighbours repairs at most one pair that stands in the wrong order, so count the pairs.
Match the k-th bead of a colour in the first row with the k-th bead of that colour in the second row; never swap equal colours.
After the matching, count the inversions of the target positions with a Fenwick tree.

explanation: The k-th bead of every colour in the first row is matched with the k-th bead of that colour in the second row. The answer is the number of inversions of the matched target positions, counted with a Fenwick tree.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def bit_add(t, i, x):
    n = len(t) - 1
    while i <= n:
        t[i] += x
        i += i & -i

def bit_sum(t, i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += t[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
b = list(map(int, input().split()))

where = {}
for j, v in enumerate(b):
    where.setdefault(v, []).append(j)
used = {}
t = [0] * (n + 1)
inv = 0
for i in range(n):
    k = used.get(a[i], 0)
    used[a[i]] = k + 1
    p = where[a[i]][k] + 1
    inv += i - bit_sum(t, p)
    bit_add(t, p, 1)
print(inv)
